subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Just-World Hypothesis: Bad Things Happen to Bad People?
description: A fast breakdown of The Just-World Hypothesis: Bad Things Happen to Bad People? for builders.

hook.text: A crime victim is asked: 'What were you wearing?' The question implies they caused their own misfortune.

buildup.text: Just-world hypothesis: the belief that people get what they deserve – good things happen to good people, bad things to.

discovery.text: Melvin Lerner (1980) proved it experimentally: observers blamed innocent victims more when they couldn't help them.

twist.text: It's psychologically protective: if bad things happen randomly, anyone could be next.

climax.text: It drives victim-blaming, poverty stigma, & resistance to systemic reform.

punchline.text: The world isn't just. Pretending it is harms the people who need help most.

quiz.question: Why do people blame victims according to the just-world hypothesis?
options: Blaming victims preserves the comforting illusion that the world is fair

details.summary: The just world hypothesis is the belief that people generally get what they deserve. It leads to victim-blaming because the alternative—that bad things happen to good people randomly—is psychologically threatening.
details.whyItMatters: This belief distorts legal judgments, social policy, and personal empathy by attributing misfortune to the character of the victim rather than circumstance.
takeaways: Believing the world is fair leads to blaming victims for their suffering
The hypothesis protects the believer's sense of safety and control
Awareness of this bias improves empathy and fairness in judgment

faq.question: How does the just world hypothesis lead to victim blaming?
faq.answer: If you believe the world is fair, then someone suffering must have done something to deserve it. Blaming the victim restores the comforting illusion that bad things only happen to bad people.

faq.question: Why is the just world hypothesis psychologically appealing?
faq.answer: It provides an illusion of control and predictability. If the world is fair, you can protect yourself by being good—which is more comforting than accepting randomness.
